title: Breaking the SFT Plateau: Multimodal Structured Reinforcement Learning for Chart-to-Code
one_liner: When teaching a model to turn charts into code, supervised learning hits a wall; using rewards that check both the code and the visual output breaks through it.
lead: Imagine teaching a person to turn a bar chart into spreadsheet code. You can show them many examples, and they improve at first because each example teaches them a new pattern they have not seen before. But eventually, all the easy patterns are memorized, and new examples show only rare edge cases and tiny variations — the learning slows to a halt. This paper shows that adding a reward system that grades the code two ways (does the code work? does it draw the right picture?) lets the model jump over that wall and keep improving.

paras: Chart-to-code is hard because the model has to see a visual image, understand what it shows (which rows, which bars, which colors matter), and then write code that makes the exact same picture when it runs. It is not enough to write code that is syntactically correct; the code has to draw the right thing.

When you train with supervised learning (showing examples and correcting the code word-by-word), the model learns quickly at first. But after eating millions of examples, each new example teaches the model less and less. Researchers call this the plateau: more data stops helping.

callout.html: Supervised fine-tuning alone runs out of steam; the model plateaus because it has no way to learn from its own mistakes.

steps.text: Train the model on chart-code pairs until it hits the plateau.
Check each line of generated code for syntax and chart-specific rules.
Run the code, render the chart, compare pixels to the ground truth.
Score progress on code quality and visual match separately.
Train the model to maximize both scores, pushing past the plateau.

paras: Instead of just correcting the model word-by-word from examples, the paper adds a second kind of teaching: rewards. These rewards do not come from human annotation; they are computed automatically by running the code and checking if the picture looks right.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: visual alignment score
hidden.name: How well the rendered code matches the chart
paras: This is the paper's new measurement. It is not just syntax or correctness; it is the visual distance between what the model's code draws and what the real chart looks like. A model-based reward system reads the generated code, runs it, captures the picture, and measures the pixel-level similarity to the ground truth.

The paper uses this hidden score to steer training. As the model learns to write code, it does not just try to match example solutions word-for-word; it also learns to make pictures that look like the target.

heat.caption: Darker means more directly tied to passing the visual test.

reads.html: The visual alignment score answers one question: if I run this code, will the picture on the screen look like the target? The higher the score, the closer the match.

The paper introduces a model-based reward that assesses structural similarity between rendered outputs and ground-truth charts by comparing visual features, providing direction on which way to nudge the weights for optimization.

mechanism.h2: Why breaking two rewards breaks the plateau
paras: Supervised learning hits a wall because the model sees examples but only learns one kind of feedback: whether each word matches the reference code. After millions of examples, there is no new pattern left to find; the model has memorized the correspondences it will ever see.

The paper adds a second channel: visual rewards. These are not based on matching words; they are based on checking if the rendered picture looks right. This gives the model a completely new learning signal. When the model tweaks the code in a way that makes the picture closer to the target — even if those tweaks are not in any training example — the visual reward still catches it and says so. The model learns to maximize picture-similarity, not just word-similarity. This is a new direction to optimize, so training can escape the plateau.

The two-stage curriculum is the second move. First, the model optimizes using only code-level rewards (syntax, chart-specific rules). This teaches it to write valid code. Then, visual rewards are turned on, and the model learns to make pretty pictures. By staging them, early training focuses on correctness, and late training focuses on visual polish. Together, these two changes let the model go from stuck to progressing again.

stages.s: Update model weights via both rewards

math.words: total_reward = alpha times code_reward plus beta times visual_reward
symbols: combined reward score for the generated code
score from rule-based code checks: 0 to 100
score from comparing rendered chart to target: 0 to 100

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Generated code has one syntax error and draws almost the right picture.
Code reward: 40 out of 100 (broken syntax is penalized).
Visual reward: 85 out of 100 (the bars are right, axis labels are off by a few pixels).
Because both rewards matter equally, the model learns to fix both the syntax and the visual details.

math.note: The model optimizes both rewards together, so training can progress even when the code-only signal saturates.

charts.title: Supervised learning only (plateau)
charts.note: More training data stops helping after a point.

charts.title: Supervised + reinforcement learning (break through)
charts.note: Reinforcement learning lifts performance past the supervised ceiling.

items.html: If the rendering engine is slow or unreliable, the visual feedback is garbled, and the model learns nonsense. The paper mitigates this by using a fast, deterministic renderer.

If code quality and visual match point in opposite directions (make the picture perfect, or make the code clean?), the model has no clear direction. The paper stages the training so code comes first, then visual polish. By weighting them separately (let us call them w_code and w_visual), the paper can raise one weight, train, then raise the other.

If the visual reward checks only pixel-level similarity, the model might learn to fake nearby pixels (adversarial perturbations) rather than writing good code. The paper uses multiple reward signals to make this harder.

If you set the code-reward weight or the visual-reward weight badly, the model ignores one reward and optimizes the other. The paper uses ablation studies to find good values, but tuning is still required for new datasets.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small benchmark of 100 chart-code pairs. Train a model on 80 pairs until supervised learning plateaus (accuracy stops improving). Then apply reinforcement learning with code + visual rewards. Measure accuracy again.
demo.closing: The demo must show a measurable jump in accuracy (at least 3–5 points) after turning on reinforcement learning, proving that visual rewards unlock learning past the supervised ceiling.
